title: Why Can't Anyone Stop These 4 Animals People Brought In?
question: Why can't anyone stop the animals people brought in?
summary: Hippos in Colombia, carp in America's rivers, cane toads across Australia and African bees across the Americas: four animals people brought in on purpose, and why none of them can be stopped.
style: Ink-and-cut-paper editorial storybook illustration, layered torn paper with ink contour lines and paper grain, muted warm palette, tropical Queensland sugar-cane country.

intro.text: You'd think an animal brought in on purpose could be taken back out.
In October 1957, near Rio Claro in Brazil, a local beekeeper noticed the queen excluders on some hive boxes and removed them.
Four animals, four countries, each brought in by people who thought they had a reason.
So why can't anyone stop them?

beats.text: Near Puerto Triunfo, Álvaro Molina was fishing when something moved beneath his canoe and spilled him into the water.
It was a hippo, a female that had recently given birth.
In the 1980s, Pablo Escobar imported four hippos for the private zoo on his estate.
When he was killed in 1993, most of his animals went to zoos. The hippos were too difficult to capture, so they stayed.
In the Magdalena River basin, nothing hunts them, and a 2022 study estimated that around 170 now roam free.
Sterilization and sending them to zoos have not worked, and Colombia has approved plans to cull up to 80.
In 2015, a 19-year-old being towed on an inner tube on the Mississippi was struck in the face by a leaping carp, and it broke his nose.
Silver carp leap up to fifteen feet out of the water when a boat spooks them.
In the 1970s, they were brought to American fish ponds to keep the water clear of algae.
They got into the rivers, and with no native fish big enough to eat them, they spread.
In parts of the Mississippi and Illinois rivers, they now make up more than ninety-five percent of the fish.
And they are about ten miles from the electric barriers that stand between them and the Great Lakes.
In 1935, Queensland's Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations released 2,400 cane toads to eat the beetles attacking its sugar cane.
beats.image: a crowd of brown cane toads spilling from wooden crates onto the edge of a sugar-cane field in the 1930s, a man in a hat watching

beats.text: No one had checked whether the toads would even eat those beetles.
beats.image: a single cane toad on bare soil looking up at tall cane stalks, a beetle far out of reach near the top

beats.text: They could not reach them: the beetles lived high on the cane stalks.
beats.image: close view of a scarab beetle clinging high on a sugar-cane stalk, the ground far below

beats.text: In 1936, entomologist Walter Froggatt warned that the toad, with no enemies and breeding all year, could become as great a pest as the rabbit.
beats.image: a 1930s entomologist in a waistcoat writing a letter at a desk lit by a lamp, a jar holding a toad beside him

beats.text: One bite can kill the predators that try to eat it, from northern quolls to freshwater crocodiles.
beats.image: a small spotted quoll creeping toward a large cane toad at night in dry grass, tension in the frame, no gore

beats.text: And the toads are speeding up, now moving west by as much as sixty kilometres a year.
beats.image: a wave of cane toads crossing a red dirt road at dusk toward the west, the outback stretching ahead

beats.text: Back to that beekeeper. When he removed the excluders, twenty-six African queens and their swarms flew into the forest.
They had been brought from South Africa in 1956 to breed bees that would make more honey in Brazil's heat.
Instead, they crossed with local bees, and the hybrids kept the African bees' fierce defence.
They chase people as far as 400 metres, and far more of them sting.
They spread through South America, reached Mexico in 1985 and Texas in 1990.
In 1993 came the first recorded death from their stings in the United States.
And wherever they arrive, they breed with gentler bees until the gentler bees disappear.

outro.text: Each one landed somewhere with nothing to stop it, and spread faster than anyone moved to stop it.
It started with twenty-six queens near Rio Claro. Their descendants have since been found as far north as Utah.
